McKinnon’s arguments are complemented by Pitjantjatjara Indigenous Social Research professor Barry Judd’s ‘Sporting Intervention: The Northern Territory National Emergency Response and Papunya Football’ (2017). Judd considers the racialised tensions of central Australian football in terms of settler colonialism, arguing that settlers’ historically ‘insatiable desire to acquire land’ was ‘rendered rational and natural by a simultaneous discursive elimination of Indigenous people’. He argues that racist othering served to ‘de-humanise, displace and ultimately disremember’ Indigenous people, and that Anglo-Australian nationalism demanded the ‘discursive elimination’ of Aboriginal people ‘from narratives of national identity’. 38 Despite the ‘progressive politics of 1967–1996’ which enacted ‘profound change’ for the Luritja and Pintupi peoples of Papunya, and saw ‘a flourishing of cultural output and a reassertion of Indigenous identity’, Judd argues that the 2007 Intervention reignited and revalidated a discursive othering. In terms of local sport, this was manifested in the largely nonIndigenous hostility towards Papunya teams and spectators visiting Alice Springs for the Central Australian Football League matches.39

Yet, like McKinnon and Moreton-Robinson, Judd argues that Papunya peoples resisted and evaded this reprisal of ‘discursive elimination’. Instead they formed their own Wilurarra Tjutaku Football League (WTFL), which is not just a separate competition, but more significantly reflects a distinct style of game: ‘On Country’ football. Judd explains that ‘On Country’ football reflects Papunya customs and values: there is minimal touching and body contact, style of play is prioritised over winning, stress is placed on the importance of family, scores are not kept but instead ‘negotiated by Elders’, and ‘prize monies [are] distributed in such a way that all teams win’ to ensure that all players can ‘“save face”’. 40 Thus Judd concludes that while the Intervention made older eliminationist discourses ‘socially permissible and politically viable’ again, the creation of the WTFL represents the way in which Aboriginal people could ‘disengage from Anglo-Australia by deciding to go their own way’. 41 McKinnon would read
